passage:
Paragraph A
On a bare Arctic hillside on the island of Spitsbergen, a concrete wedge juts out of the snow. Behind it a tunnel runs a hundred and twenty metres into the rock, ending in three chambers cut deep inside the mountain. There are no permanent staff, no laboratory and very little to see. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault is not a research station but a warehouse — the last copy, held far from anywhere, of the crops that feed the world.

Paragraph B
The vault exists because the seeds it protects are unusually fragile as a form of property. A book can be reprinted and a painting photographed, but a crop variety exists only as living tissue, and living tissue dies. Around seventeen hundred seed banks operate around the world, most attached to universities or agriculture ministries, and each holds material found nowhere else. They are also, individually, vulnerable in the most ordinary ways: a failed freezer, a burst pipe, a budget cut, a war. Svalbard was built to be the copy that survives whatever removes the original.

Paragraph C
The site was chosen for its dullness. Spitsbergen is remote but reachable by scheduled flight; it is politically stable; and the mountain is high enough that even a substantial rise in sea level would leave the entrance dry. Most importantly, the rock is permanently frozen. The chambers are chilled to minus eighteen degrees by mechanical refrigeration, but if the power failed the surrounding permafrost would hold them well below freezing for weeks, buying time for a repair. The building is engineered, in effect, to fail slowly.

Paragraph D
What arrives is not a jar of loose seed. Each deposit is sealed in a foil packet, boxed, and logged, and the depositing institution keeps the only key: Svalbard stores the boxes but never opens them, and cannot lend, sell or study the contents. The arrangement is deliberately closer to a safe-deposit box than to a library. It also sidesteps a long-running political argument about who owns plant genetic material, since ownership never changes hands at all.

Paragraph E
The vault has been used in earnest exactly once. A seed bank in Aleppo held one of the world's great collections of wheat, barley and lentils adapted to dry conditions, and it had sent duplicates to Svalbard as a routine precaution. When the Syrian civil war made the site impossible to operate, researchers who had relocated to Lebanon and Morocco requested their own deposits back. The boxes were returned, the seeds were grown out, fresh seed was harvested, and new duplicates were sent north again. The system worked precisely as intended, and almost nobody had expected to see it tested so soon.

Paragraph F
Seeds do not keep forever even at minus eighteen. Different species age at very different rates: some remain viable for centuries, while others fade within decades. Every accession therefore has to be tested periodically for germination, and once the proportion that will sprout falls too low, the depositing bank must grow the variety out and replace the sample. This regeneration is the expensive, unglamorous heart of the whole enterprise, and it happens not in Svalbard but back at the hundreds of ordinary institutions that own the material.

Paragraph G
The collection is also incomplete in a way that is not always understood. It is strongest in the seed crops that dominate world trade — wheat, rice, maize, beans — and much weaker in plants that are not grown from seed at all. Potatoes, cassava, bananas and yams are propagated from tubers or cuttings, and cannot simply be dried and frozen; they are kept alive in field plots or in test tubes, at far greater cost and far greater risk. For a significant part of the food supply, no equivalent of Svalbard yet exists.

Paragraph H
It is tempting to read the vault as a monument to pessimism, and it is often photographed that way — a bunker against catastrophe, standing in the snow. The people who run it describe something more modest. The likeliest threats to a seed collection are not asteroids or nuclear war but the slow, unremarkable failures of institutions: money that stops arriving, equipment that is not replaced, a country that stops caring. Svalbard is insurance against ordinary neglect. That it looks like a doomsday shelter is a matter of geography, not of intent.

(Glossary: permafrost: ground that stays frozen all year round; accession: a single sample of one crop variety held in a seed bank; germination: the sprouting of a seed into a young plant.)
